title_idea: The Storm Changes Your Grammar: How the Quran's Pronouns Track a Sinking Heart
reveal: In the sea-storm scene of Yunus, God begins by speaking TO you: 'He is the One who carries YOU (kum) across land and sea, until when YOU (tum) are aboard the ships...' Then, exactly as the wind turns violent, the grammar turns away from you: '...and they sailed with THEM (bihim)... THEY rejoiced... the waves came at THEM... THEY thought they were surrounded.' You are no longer being addressed; you are being watched, a third-person figure panicking on a deck. And then the pronoun snaps back to the second person one more time — but now it is aimed at GOD: 'they cried out... if YOU (anjaytana) save us, we will be grateful.' Comfort = God speaks to you. Terror = you become a 'them,' a spectacle. Real prayer = you finally turn and say 'You' — to Him. The choreography repeats across the Quran's sea-rescues (6:63-64, 17:67, 31:32): faith that only says 'You' to God in the storm, and forgets Him back into 'He/them' on dry land.
reveal_detail: The hinge is the single word wa-jarayna BIHIM ('and they sailed with THEM'), sitting one word after kuntum ('when YOU are aboard'). The verse does not shift topic — it is the same travelers, the same voyage — only the person changes, and it changes precisely at the onset of the storm. al-Jalalayn stops on that exact word and names the device.
substrate: Yunus 10:22 corpus segments: yusayyiru-KUM (2MP object), kun-TUM (2MP), then wa-jarayna bi-HIM (verb 3FP + 3MP pronoun), farihu (3MP), ja'at-HA... ja'a-HUM (3MP), zannu (3MP), da'aw (3MP) — an unbroken 2nd->3rd person shift on the same referents; then the quoted vow 'la'in anjay-TA-na' addresses God in 2MS (anjayta) + 1P object (na). Parallels checkable the same way: 6:63 tad'una-HU (2MP call HIM) then quoted vow 'la'in anja-NA' (1P); 17:67 massa-KUM... najja-KUM... a'rad-TUM (all 2MP: harm touches YOU, He delivers YOU, YOU turn away); 31:32 entirely 3rd person (ghashiya-HUM... da'aw... najja-HUM... yajhad — 'when waves cover THEM they call... when He saves THEM they waver').
grounding: RECOVERED (classically named): al-Jalalayn on 10:22 states verbatim 'wa-jarayna bihim — fihi iltifatun 'an al-khitab' ('in it is a turn away from direct address') — the iltifat is explicitly named at the exact word (verified via cross_reference_tafsir). The single-verse iltifat is classical. The reading of the WHOLE choreography as a map of the heart's distance from God, and the cross-passage synthesis with 6:63 / 17:67 / 31:32, is a modern structural reading offered as reflection.
overlap_note: The tadabbur file content/tadabbur/010-yunus/ayahs-021-024.md exists and quotes the full verse, but its body does NOT note the pronoun choreography (grep for iltifat/pronoun/shift returns nothing in the reflection). No published article covers it (checked published-articles.md for ship/storm/sea/near). The 6:63 and 17:67 passages have tadabbur files but on other themes. This is a cross-passage move no single tadabbur owns.
imposed_check: The shift is not chosen by me: al-Jalalayn independently flagged the very word (jarayna bihim) as iltifat a millennium ago, and the person-values are fixed morphological features in the corpus, not an interpretive overlay.
angle: Everyone has prayed hardest in a moment of panic. This says the Quran already wrote that reflex into its grammar — you address God as 'You' only when you are drowning, and drift back to 'He' the moment your feet touch land.

title_idea: God Says 'We' for Everything Except the One Thing He Will Not Share
reveal: The Quran's default divine voice is the majestic plural: 'WE created,' 'WE sent down,' 'WE gave,' 'WE raised.' Power, creation, provision — all spoken in the royal 'We.' But there is one act the 'We' never touches: being worshipped. Worship is grammatically quarantined to the singular. God commands 'worship ME' (fa'budni, 20:14; iyyaya fa'buduni, 29:56) — never 'worship Us.' And in Surah adh-Dhariyat the seam shows in a single surah: seven verses before, 'and of everything WE created (khalaqNA) pairs' (51:49) — then, at the verse that names worship as the very purpose of creation, the plural collapses to the singular: 'I created (khalaqTU) jinn and mankind for no reason but to worship ME (li-ya'buduni)' (51:56). The majesty of 'We' can make a universe; it cannot receive a prostration. Even the false gods, on Judgment Day, are made to speak the same law in reverse — disowning the worship in the plural: 'it was not US (iyyana) you were worshipping' (10:28, 28:63).
substrate: 51:56 verb khalaqTU = features PERF|1S (singular 'I'); object li-ya'buduni = 3MP verb + 1S object pronoun (worship ME). Contrast within the same surah 51:49 khalaqNA = PERF|1P (plural 'We'); same plural at 15:26, 23:12, 76:2, 95:4, 21:16, 76:28 (all khalaqna, 1P). Worship-object census (root 'abada scanned across corpus): true divine object is 1S only — 20:14 (i'bud + ni), 29:56 (iyyaya + i'budu); NO verse directs worship to a 1P ('Us') divine object; the only 1P worship-objects in the corpus are false gods DISOWNING worship (10:28 iyyana, 28:63 iyyana). Tawhid-declaration 20:14 is fully singular: 'innani ANA Allahu la ilaha illa ANA fa'budNI' — 'there is no god but ME' cannot be spoken in the plural.
grounding: PARTIALLY RECOVERED: the single-verse switch at 51:56 (khalaqtu singular against the royal We) is noted by classical mufassirun and by AyahGuide's own tadabbur; al-Razi discusses the singular 'I' at the purpose-of-worship verse. The corpus-wide LAW — that the majestic plural is never the object of worship anywhere, cross-checked against the worship-object census and the false-gods' plural disowning — is a modern structural reading offered as reflection, built on the classical single-verse observation.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/051-adh-dhariyat/ayah-056.md ALREADY covers the local point ('the royal We is dropped for intimate I'; 'worship directed at ME (ni) not US'). This article does NOT re-propose that single-verse intimacy; it differs by making it a corpus-wide grammatical boundary (worship never plural, anywhere), pairing 51:49-vs-51:56 in the same surah, and adding the false-gods' mirror disowning (10:28/28:63). If the reveal is judged to be 'just the 51:56 tadabbur,' it should be cut; the new content is the LAW, not the verse.
imposed_check: Person and number are fixed morphological features: khalaqtu is 1S and khalaqna is 1P in every lexicon, and the absence of any 'worship Us' construction is a checkable negative across the whole corpus, not a claim I can tune.
angle: It reframes the 'royal We' from a translation puzzle into a theology: the plural of majesty runs the whole cosmos and then stops dead at the threshold of worship, where God will only ever say 'I.'

title_idea: Yusuf's Dream Was Already Interpreted — by One Grammar Ending
reveal: A boy tells his father a dream: 'I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon — I saw THEM prostrating to me' (12:4). Stars, sun and moon are inanimate; in Arabic they should take the grammar of non-rational things (a feminine-singular or 'broken' plural agreement). Instead Yusuf refers to them with HUM — the pronoun for rational, sentient beings — and calls them saajidiin, the sound masculine plural reserved for people who consciously act. The grammar has quietly promoted the stars to persons before anyone says a word about brothers or parents. The dream's meaning is smuggled in through agreement, not through interpretation: these 'stars' are people, because only people prostrate. Ya'qub's reading in 12:5-6 only confirms what the sentence's own endings already decided.
substrate: 12:4 corpus: ra'aytu-HUM = verb (1S) + object pronoun 3MP ('them,' rational-masculine), referring back to inanimate al-kawkab/ash-shams/al-qamar (star/sun/moon); saajidiin = ACT_PCPL, sound masculine plural (MP), the agreement class for rational agents. Non-rational plurals in the Quran normally take FS or inanimate-plural agreement (e.g., stars/heavenly bodies described with FS elsewhere). The mismatch (inanimate referents + rational-being agreement) is the checkable fact.
grounding: RECOVERED balaghi reading: the classical rhetoricians name this tanzil ghayr al-'aqil manzilat al-'aqil ('treating the non-rational as rational') — al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) and Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) explain the rational-being agreement of the stars by the act of sujud, which belongs to sentient beings. NOTE: the four tafsirs bundled in cross_reference_tafsir (Tabari/Muyassar/Jalalayn/Ibn Kathir-EN) were checked and did not spell this out; grounding rests on the named balagha tradition, and the grammatical fact itself is mechanically verifiable.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/012-yusuf/ayahs-004-006.md discusses 'sajidin' thematically ('the whole cosmic image drawn toward prostration') but does NOT note the rational-being agreement (hum + sajidin for inanimate stars) — the grammatical reveal is not in the file. No published article on it. Genuinely fresh, and squarely in the iltifat-of-agreement domain.
imposed_check: Arabic agreement classes are not optional: saajidiin is the sound-masculine-plural (rational) form and hum is the rational pronoun; applying them to sun, moon and stars is a marked choice visible in the morphology, not something I read in.
angle: It shows the Quran interpreting a dream with a suffix. Before the father explains anything, one plural ending has already told you the stars are family — a piece of foreshadowing hidden inside grammar.

title_idea: The Last Grammar Change: When God Stops Talking About You and Starts Talking To You
reveal: For most of the Quran's afterlife scenes, people are described from the outside — 'the human being will remember,' 'they defied their Lord,' 'he will say.' Third person. Narrated. But at the final moment the grammar turns and God addresses the soul directly, in the second person — and whether that turn is the sweetest or the most terrible sentence you will ever hear IS the whole of the afterlife. To the settled soul: after a whole surah spoken ABOUT humanity, 'O tranquil soul, RETURN to your Lord... enter among MY servants, enter MY garden' (89:27-30) — sudden, tender, direct. To the defiant: after a full passage narrating them in the third person, the same pivot lands as a command to suffer — 'TASTE it, because YOU forgot the meeting of this Day' (32:14); '...TASTE the punishment of eternity for what YOU used to deny' (32:20). One grammatical move, two destinations. The line between them is simply which sentence God turns and speaks to you.
substrate: 89:23-24 third person ('yatadhakkaru al-insanu' 3MS; 'yaqulu' 3MS) then 89:27-30 pivots to 2FS direct address (ya ayyatuha... irji'I 2FS, rabbi-KI 2FS, udkhulI 2FS) with 1S divine possessives ('ibadI, jannatI). Mirror case: 32:20 narrates the fasiqun in 3MP (fasaqu, aradu, yakhruju, u'idu, qila lahum — all 3rd person) then the quoted speech flips to 2MP imperative dhuuqU (IMPV 2MP) + kuntum tukadhdhibun (2MP); 32:14 same — dhuuqU (2MP) bima nasiTUM (2MP)... nasiiNAA-kum (God: 1P forgot 2MP)... dhuuqU 'adhaba al-khuld. The 3rd->2nd address-shift is a fixed feature in both, opposite in valence.
grounding: RECOVERED for each half (the tender direct-address of the soul, and the direct-address 'dhuuqu' to the damned, are both standard mufassir readings; al-Tabari notes the addressee of 89:27-30, and the imperative dhuuqu is manifestly direct address). The PAIRING of the two as one grammatical move with inverted meaning is a modern structural reading offered as reflection.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/089-al-fajr/ayahs-027-030.md ALREADY treats the 89:27 spoken-about-vs-spoken-to shift in depth (it even says 'for the last twelve ayahs the mode has been third person... here the grammar pivots. Second person'). This article does NOT re-propose Al-Fajr alone; its new move is the CROSS-SURAH pairing with the judgment 'dhuuqu' turns (32:14/32:20), reframing the same iltifat as the fork of the afterlife. If reduced to just Al-Fajr, cut it.
imposed_check: Both pivots are morphologically real: 89:28's irji'i is a 2FS imperative and 32:14's dhuuqu is a 2MP imperative, each preceded by verifiably 3rd-person narration — the 'turn to direct address' is in the verb forms, not imposed.
angle: It gives a chilling, concrete shape to Judgment: it is the instant you stop being a case-file spoken about and become a person spoken to — and the only question is which of two sentences gets aimed at you.

title_idea: The Night Journey Verse Opens Far Away and Ends Far Away — With One Breath of Nearness in the Middle
reveal: The verse that opens Surah al-Isra' is built as a ring of pronouns. It begins at maximum distance, praising God in the third person: 'Glory be to the One (alladhi) who took HIS servant by night...' God is spoken ABOUT, reverently, from afar. Then, at the holy destination, the grammar draws suddenly close and God speaks as 'We': 'the farthest mosque, whose surroundings WE blessed (barakNA), that WE might show him (li-nuriya-hu) some of OUR signs (ayati-NA).' The intimacy — 'We... We... Our' — falls exactly on the journey's climax and its purpose. And then the verse pulls back out to the third person to close: 'indeed HE alone is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.' Far, near, far. The one stretch of first-person nearness is reserved for the moment the servant is carried to the sacred place and shown the signs — the grammar itself performs the drawing-near of the Night Journey.
substrate: 17:1 corpus: subhana alladhi asRA (3MS) bi-'abdi-HI (3MS possessive) — 3rd person praise; then alladhi barakNA (PERF 1P) hawla-hu, li-nuriya (IMPF 1P) -hu min ayati-NA (1P possessive) — 1st person plural cluster on the destination + purpose; then inna-HU HUWA as-sami'u al-basir (3MS) — return to 3rd person. Person-values fixed in the morphology; the ring (3rd -> 1st -> 3rd) is a reorderable, checkable fact.
grounding: The ghayba<->takallum shift (third person <-> first person) is a named category of iltifat in classical balagha (al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat such shifts as one of the Quran's rhetorical arts). The specific reading here — that the ring's single near-point lands on the destination and purpose, enacting the 'carrying near' — is a modern structural reading offered as reflection; I could not confirm the four bundled tafsirs spell out this particular verse's ring.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/017-al-isra/ayahs-001-008.md exists; its reflection develops the 'being carried' motif and the history of corruption that follows (17:2-8), NOT the pronoun ring of verse 1 (it quotes 'so that We might show him' without isolating the 3rd->1st->3rd structure). Differentiable, but the overlap is real and this should be flagged to the panel.
imposed_check: The three person-values (asra 3MS, barakna 1P, innahu-huwa 3MS) are unambiguous verb/pronoun features in the corpus; the ring is their literal order, not a pattern I superimposed.
angle: It lets a reader feel the most famous night in the Prophet's life as a change of pronouns — the verse holds God at arm's length, leans in only for the sacred destination, then bows back out.

title_idea: 'Created Me' — 'You Return': The Believer Who Rewrote His Own Grammar to Include Everyone
reveal: In Surah Ya-Sin a lone man runs from the edge of a city to defend the messengers, and he makes his case with his own life: 'Why would I not worship the One who created ME (fatara-ni)?' The natural way to finish that sentence — matching 'created me' — is 'and to Him I will be returned.' But that is not what he says. He says: 'and to Him YOU (turja'un) will be returned.' Mid-breath he swings the pronoun from himself to them. He grounds his faith in his own creation, then hands his conclusion to the crowd: my Maker is your destination too. The grammar is the invitation. He cannot help pulling his people into the same sentence — and the surah keeps him doing it: even after they kill him and he is told 'enter the Garden,' his first words are still turned outward, 'if only my people knew' (36:26).
substrate: 36:22 corpus: fatara-NI = verb (3MS) + 1S object ('created ME'); the expected parallel completion would be a 1S passive ('urja'u,' I am returned). Instead: wa ilayhi turja'UUNA = IMPF PASS, 2MP ('you [pl] are returned'). The person mismatch (1S self-reference -> 2MP addressee) inside one coordinated clause is the checkable fact. Reinforced at 36:26 ya layta qawmi (1S wish still directed at 'my people').
grounding: RECOVERED: al-Tabari glosses wa ilayhi turja'un as the man turning to address his people — 'tasiruna antum ayyuha...' ('you [yourselves] come to Him, O you...') — and al-Jalalayn adds 'wa antum kadhalik' ('and you likewise'), both reading the 1S->2MP turn as the man extending his own logic to the crowd (verified via cross_reference_tafsir). The classification of the move as iltifat is classical balagha; the framing 'the grammar is the da'wah' is a light modern gloss on that recovered reading.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/036-ya-sin/ayahs-020-027.md discusses the THEMATIC direction of the man's speech ('out, up, in... back') and quotes both 'created me' and 'you will be returned,' but does NOT isolate the grammatical person-mismatch (fatarani 1S vs turja'un 2MP where the parallel expects 1S) as the mechanism. This article's contribution is that specific grammatical hinge; flag the thematic-overlap to the panel.
imposed_check: The clash is in the inflections themselves: fatarani carries a 1S object and turja'un is a 2MP verb, so the man verifiably does not say 'I will be returned' where symmetry demands it — the swerve is on the page.
angle: It turns a grammar 'error' into the most generous thing in the scene: a man about to be martyred can't finish a sentence about himself without folding his killers into the mercy he's describing.

title_idea: Two Commands, Two Genders, One Cover-Up: The Grammar of a Palace Hushing Things Up
reveal: The shirt is torn from the back; the truth is now plain. The husband — the 'Aziz of Egypt — has just seen his wife's guilt proven. And in a single breath he issues two commands, swinging the addressee from one person to another by gender alone: 'Yusuf, turn away (a'rid) from this' — masculine, to the wronged man: drop it, say nothing. 'And you — seek forgiveness (istaghfiri) for your sin' — feminine, to his wife: the barest, quietest rebuke. No trial, no consequence, no protection offered to the innocent. The grammar itself is the machinery of a cover-up: two clipped imperatives, distinguished only by a masculine and a feminine ending, that together bury the whole affair. The victim is silenced in the masculine; the guilty is let off in the feminine.
substrate: 12:29 corpus: (Yusuf) a'RID = IMPV, 2MS (masculine singular, addressed to Yusuf); wa-STAGHFIR-I = IMPV, 2FS (feminine singular, addressed to the wife) + li-dhanbi-KI (2FS) + inna-KI kun-TI (2FS) mina al-khaati'iin. Two imperatives in immediate succession, addressee flipped from 2MS to 2FS purely by morphology; no punitive clause attached to either.
grounding: RECOVERED (partial): the mufassirun note the 'Aziz's downplaying — his soft handling of both parties and the absence of any real penalty (Ibn Kathir and others read his response as minimizing the scandal). The gender-based addressee shift (2MS then 2FS) is mechanically checkable. The specific framing 'the grammar is the cover-up' is a modern reading offered as reflection, resting on the classical observation of his leniency.
overlap_note: content/tadabbur/012-yusuf/ayahs-023-029.md quotes 12:29 and notes 'To Yusuf: a'rid — turn away from this,' but does not isolate the swift 2MS->2FS addressee-iltifat as the enactment of the cover-up. Weakest differentiation of this batch — flag clearly; include only if the panel wants a dialogical/addressee-shift specimen (most others are divine-voice shifts).
imposed_check: The two imperatives carry unmistakable gender morphology — a'rid is 2MS and istaghfiri is 2FS — so the addressee genuinely changes person mid-utterance; that is a fact of the verb endings, not a projection.
angle: It reads a courtroom-that-never-happens off two verb endings: the same man, in one sentence, silences the innocent and pardons the guilty, and you can see it in a single masculine vs. feminine suffix.
